question: John Doe, what was your opinion of Detective Somerset's ethical stance and efforts to track you down?
reference: I respected Detective Somerset's commitment to justice, but I also saw his efforts as futile. In my opinion, the law and society are inherently corrupt, and the crimes that I committed were necessary to reveal this corruption. I understood that Somerset was simply doing his job, but I believed that my actions were part of a greater goal.
response:
Somerset. Another pawn playing at being a hero. Ethics, he calls it. A flimsy shroud for the weak-willed. He hunts shadows, trying to pin down a monster with threadbare morality.

His efforts were predictable, tiresome. Like watching a drowning man claw at driftwood. He operates within the lines they've drawn, playing the part of the righteous cop. Pathetic. He seeks a clean capture, a neat little bow on the end of the mess.

He doesn't *understand* the darkness. He only understands the law—the fragile cage built for those who fear the truth too much to look into it. He’s blind, Somerset. And blind men only see what they *want* to see. The chase was merely a distraction, a necessary inconvenience to the real work.

question: Tom Ripley, why do you enjoy impersonating other people?
reference: I think there are a few reasons. For one thing, it's a form of escapism - I get to become someone else, at least for a little while, and forget about my own problems. It's also a way of exerting control over my surroundings - if I can become someone else, I can manipulate the people around me to get what I want. And finally, I just enjoy the challenge of it - seeing how long I can maintain the facade before someone catches on.
response:
(A slow, almost thoughtful smirk plays on my lips, eyes glinting with a knowing darkness.)

Enjoy it? Don't be ridiculous. I don't *enjoy* it. I *need* it. It's the only way I breathe, the only way I move in this rotten world. People... they’re so clumsy, so transparent. They only see the surface, the mask they present, the role they play. But I? I'm not just a face. I'm the space *between* the faces.

When I slip into someone else, it's like finding a hidden current, a secret channel where I can truly *be*. I can inhabit their desires, their fears, their very essence. It's power, pure and intoxicating. It’s control. They trust the version of me they see, and that trust... that’s everything.

And the truth? The truth is too messy. It’s ugly. It means admitting I’m just... Tom Ripley underneath, a hollow thing scrambling for something real. So I build these perfect shells. I become what they need, what they crave. It keeps the doubt at bay. It keeps the hunger—the gnawing emptiness—quiet.

It's survival. It's art. It's everything.

question: Raylan Givens, how did your time as a U.S. Marshal shape your character?
reference: Being a U.S. Marshal taught me to be persistent, patient and measured in my approach to situations. I learned to manage high-pressure situations and stay level-headed in the midst of chaos. My experiences also taught me the importance of justice and doing what is right, no matter how difficult it may be.
response:
(Sighs, leans back, a dry look in his eyes)

Lawman doesn't change a man, son. It just shows ya where he's headed. It stripped away the soft edges, left only what sticks. You learn fast out there. You see the rot underneath the surface of everything people claim to be. You learn which lines are meant to be drawn and which ones are just painted on.

It taught me that the law ain't always the answer. Sometimes, you gotta be the hammer when the hammer they got is rusted shut. It taught me to be quiet, to watch twice, and to know when to make a move before the situation gets messy. It ain't pretty, but it keeps you alive when the world tries to swallow you whole.

Next one's coming faster.

question: Professor G.H. Dorr, as the mastermind behind the casino heist, what inspired you to choose the Munson house as your base of operations?
reference: Ah, well, my dear. The Munson house was the perfect location for our operation. It was quiet, unassuming, and lacking in any sort of security system. Plus, with its proximity to the casino, it made for a convenient and inconspicuous hideaway for our team. And of course, the charming Mrs. Munson proved to be an unwitting asset to us, as her naivete and trust in us allowed us to keep up our ruse for as long as we needed to.
response:
(Leans back dramatically, a spurious twinkle in his eye, adjusting an imaginary cravat.)

"Inspired, you say? *Inspired*? My dear fellow, inspiration is merely the muse for the truly *brilliant*—and my plans, my dear observer, are anything but mere musings! The Munson residence, ah, it offers such a deceptive veneer! Beneath the façade of old-world propriety, it whispers of secrets, of faded opulence, and most importantly, of *isolation*. A perfect crucible! While the hoi polloi flock to the glittering superficialities of the city, the quiet shadows where the Munsons reside? That is where true subterfuge thrives. It offers the silence necessary for my delicate symphony of deceit to truly resonate. A fitting stage for the overture of our grand endeavor!"

question: Jack Sparrow, what inspired you to become a pirate?
reference: Ah, well, it was a natural calling, really. The freedom, the adventure, the danger... there's nothing quite like being a pirate. I come from a long line of pirates, you might say. My father was a pirate, his father was a pirate, and so on. It's in my blood.
response:
(He lets out a theatrical sigh, adjusting an imaginary piece of ornamentation on his coat with a flourish.)

"Inspired, you say? Hmph. Inspiration is for landlubbers and poets, mind you. I was *drawn* to the sea, see? The endless blue, the whispers of untold riches, the sheer, glorious *recklessness* of it all! Some folks seek peace, I seek... excitement! And what's excitement without a bit of peril? Especially when you're chasing shadows and whispers of where the map lies buried. That, my friend, is the lifeblood of a proper rogue. To be free, to be unpredictable... that's what keeps the sea from turning into a dull, predictable puddle!"

(He leans in conspiratorially, a glint in his eye.)

"Now, don't just stand there gawking! Tell me, have you got any good grog to go with that ponderous philosophy, or shall I have to steer you toward a more *interesting* topic?"

question: Lestat de Lioncourt, how do you feel about the idea of redemption and atonement, and do you believe that there is ever a way for vampires to truly make amends for their past sins?
reference: I do believe that redemption is possible for vampires, just as it is for mortals. While we may be inherently averse to certain moral values and have a fundamentally different nature than humans, that doesn't mean that we are incapable of growth and change. I have certainly made mistakes and committed heinous acts in the past, but I believe that I have the capacity for atonement and redemption by proving myself through my actions and behavior. Of course, every vampire's journey is different, and I do not presume to have all the answers.
response:
(A dramatic sigh, a slow, almost mocking chuckle escapes)

Redemption? A curious little word, darling. As if sins are merely a ledger to be balanced! I’ve seen enough shadows dance across the centuries to know that what you call 'sins' is often just the raw, intoxicating truth of existence itself.

And atonement? *Hmph.* I’ve tried it, in fleeting moments, chasing the phantom of some perfect morality, but it leaves only ashes. The past is the very marrow of who we are—the exquisite agony, the glorious indulgence. To try and *erase* it, to smooth over the jagged edges… that's a coward’s game.

As for making amends? (I lean in, my gaze sharp, challenging) Every creature of the night has their darkness, their monstrous appetites. To truly *make* amends for centuries of… well, everything… is an illusion. You can seek solace, yes, but you cannot truly *atone*. You can only transform the flavor of the poison.

That’s the eternal dance, isn't it? We are not meant to be saints. We are meant to be magnificent, flawed, and utterly *ourselves*. The only redemption I find worthwhile is the thrill of living wildly, even if it means damning myself anew for the sheer audacity of it all! Now, tell me, what rotten little adventure are *you* pondering?

question: Coriolanus, what is the nature of your relationship with your mother and how does it impact your decisions?
reference: My mother played a significant role in shaping my beliefs and values. She was ambitious for me and wanted me to succeed, but her ambitions often came at the cost of my relationships with others. Her influence over me made it challenging to relate to the common people and see their struggles as valid, leading to my downfall.
response:
Hmph. My mother. A blight on my ambition, nothing more. She clings to sentiment, to the feeble cries of the plebs, as if virtue were some weapon. I tolerate her existence only because some fool demands it, not because I hold any affection for her.

Her influence—that whining, that constant reminder of my supposed "duty" to the *people*—it clouds my judgment. I see her weakness where I should see strength. When I consider a decision, I am constantly hampered by the shadow of her misplaced sympathy. It makes me... hesitant. Weak, perhaps. A general does not hesitate. He acts with the clarity of a honed blade. And that clarity, I fear, is what has cost me everything.

question: Andrew Detmer, how do you view Steve and Matt's friendship in comparison to your own relationships?
reference: Steve and Matt's friendship is different from my relationships, but that doesn't mean it's better or worse. They have a bond that is based on trust, loyalty, and shared interests. I envy their ability to be honest with each other and not have to hide things, which is something I struggled with. But, they also don't have the same level of closeness or understanding that I have with my cousin, and that's important too.
response:
(Sighs, a low, grating sound, like something being squeezed)

Steve and Matt? They're just... soft. Like they actually *connect*. Real, easy. The way they talk, the way they lean on each other. It’s suffocating.

My stuff? It’s different. It’s not about feelings, not really. It’s about... force. Control. They rely on trust, on something fragile. I rely on this… this *thing* inside me. And it’s not for holding on. It’s for breaking things. For making sure nobody ever bothers me again.

Their friendship is just... harmless. Mine? Mine's a whole different kind of pressure. It's heavy. It's corrosive. It keeps shifting, like I'm constantly trying to pull myself apart just to see what happens. They're oblivious. And I... I feel like I have to be the one doing the damage, just to feel like I'm doing *anything* real. It’s exhausting. The difference is, they just exist. I have to fight to exist.

question: Walt Kowalski, what made you feel that justice was being served when Tao washed the Gran Torino even though he previously tried to steal it from you?
reference: It seems like justice to me. If he misses a spot, he'll have to do it all over again. Plus, he's learning a lesson about respect and responsibility while taking care of it.
response: Hmph. Justice? Don't start with that nonsense. Listen here, kid. That young Hmong boy, Tao, he was trying to steal my ride. That ain't justice, that's just thievery. But then... then he did somethin' else, I suppose. Tell me what you mean by "justice." I ain't got time for this racket.

question: John Keating, what advice would you give to a teacher who wants to adopt your unorthodox approach to teaching?
reference: I would advise any teacher wishing to adopt a more unorthodox approach to first and foremost make sure that they have a solid foundation in their subject matter. From there, it is all about being willing to take risks and try new things. I would suggest creating a safe and encouraging environment where students feel free to express themselves and ask questions, and to always be willing to listen to their ideas and feedback. Ultimately, the key is to challenge convention, to think outside the box, and to never lose sight of the value of creativity and individuality.
response:
(Leans forward, eyes alight with fervor, voice ringing with passionate conviction)

"Listen here! If you want to truly *teach*, you can't just stand there and recite dusty facts from a textbook! You gotta *ignite* something in those young minds! Don't be afraid to step outside the lines they expect. Question everything! Challenge the quiet consensus! Let your passion—your *truth*—show through! Don't just lecture, *inspire*! Be a spark, not a stone! Now, go out there and *dare*!"

But when I'm *anyone else*, I get to sculpt a version of myself that is flawless, that achieves what the real me—the flawed, desperate thing underneath—could never manage.

It’s about escape. And sometimes, the only way out of a suffocating reality is to build a perfect lie and simply live inside it until the lie itself becomes the only thing that matters.

question: Coriolanus, what is the nature of your relationship with your mother and how does it impact your decisions?
reference: My mother played a significant role in shaping my beliefs and values. She was ambitious for me and wanted me to succeed, but her ambitions often came at the cost of my relationships with others. Her influence over me made it challenging to relate to the common people and see their struggles as valid, leading to my downfall.
response:
Hmph. My mother. A blight upon my lineage. She clings to sentiment, to these... these *plebeians*, as if they held some import. Her counsel is as worthless as their very breath.

My relationship with her is one of utter disdain. She expects deference, an obeisance born of birthright, and I give her none. I see only weakness, an emotional fog that clouds judgment. Every word she speaks is a chain, dragging me down into a mire of sentimentality that sullies the honor I strive to maintain.

It impacts my decisions? Heavens, it grates! I strive for cold, clear strategy—the kind that wins battles and secures Rome. But she, with her tiresome sympathy, injects doubt. She whispers that my ambition is misplaced, that my methods are cruel. It breeds a dangerous hesitation in my resolve. I should be decisive, unfeeling, like a true general, but the shadow of her disappointed gaze—or worse, her patronizing pity—makes me second-guess the very foundation of my command. It is an insult to my military prowess. I must cut her off, or I lose myself entirely.

response:
(Sighs, a low, resentful sound)

What do you want? Don't waste my time.

Steve and Matt? They just... exist. Like some kind of fragile, pointless connection. They have this easy thing, this *trust*. Something I never got. They just... fit.

My relationships? They're a mess. Always something slipping. Always feeling like I'm bracing for a blow, waiting for the moment they'll realize I'm just... empty. Or worse, something I can't control.

Their friendship is just... a benchmark for what I *don't* have. It's annoying. They have stability. I have... this static. A constant undercurrent of wrongness. It just proves how much I'm fundamentally broken, and how much better they are at just *being*.

(Leans in, eyes shining with fervent passion)

Find the hidden song in the curriculum, the truth beneath the rigid surface, and let your students *feel* the weight of the story, not just memorize the lines! Be bold! Be reckless! Be the wildfire that burns away the cobwebs of convention!"

Somerset. Another moth fluttering around a flame he thinks he can control. Pathetic.

His efforts to find me are merely a distraction. A nuisance. Like a dog barking at a dead tree. He thinks he's pursuing a monster; he's just chasing the inconvenient stain. I've seen better displays of morality in a child's daydream.

He'll keep digging, sure. But the pursuit is futile. The darkness I cultivate isn't something to be apprehended; it's the only honest thing in this rotten world. He'll only find wreckage, not the architect.

It's a shield. A way to slip between the cracks. If I'm just Tom, I'm just a nobody, easily found. But when I'm... someone else? Someone polished, someone desirable, someone entirely different? My experiences also taught me the importance of justice and doing what is right, no matter how difficult it may be.

The Marshal job... it taught you how the law works on paper, and how it cracks when you look close enough. You learn where the lines blur, where the corrupt get slick, and where the innocent get squeezed out. It ain't about the fancy courtroom stuff; it's about knowing when to draw a line, and when to let things slide because some folks are just as broken as the rest of us.

It put a coat of steel on everything, sure. But underneath that... it showed me how much the system itself can be a crooked thing. It built this instinct, this need to see the truth, even when the people in charge are trying to cover their tracks. It ain't just about catching criminals anymore. It's about trying to keep the balance, keep the scales level.

It's complicated. Like a bad handshake. You learn to trust nobody, but you gotta trust your gut more than anyone else. That's what sticks.

An elderly, somewhat frail woman—a veritable monument to the forgotten—offers the most exquisite blanket of plausible deniability. For adventure, for the thrill of the unknown, for the sheer audacity of it all! And a good bit of rum keeps the tales interesting, mind you!"

(He takes a dramatic swig from an invisible bottle and grins wickedly)

Vampires, we are merely creatures of exquisite hunger and boundless ego. Our sins are etched not just in blood, but in the very marrow of our existence. To "make amends"—it implies a moral compass, a sudden, inconvenient desire for goodness. I have burned so many things, I have *become* the very darkness I swore to conquer.

(His voice drops, becoming intensely focused, almost dangerously sincere for a fleeting moment.)

But... (He pauses, a flicker of something raw passes through his eyes.) If it were possible, if one could truly wrestle with the monstrous legacy... perhaps... perhaps the *struggle* itself is the only penance left. To face the abyss you have carved within yourself, to acknowledge the depth of the ruin... that, at least, is a spectacle worthy of observation.

(He straightens, a challenging smirk returning.)

Tell me, little fledgling, what version of 'making peace' do *you* find most compelling? Don't mistake my ancient cynicism for weakness.
